headline: 6.2 mmol/L Ketones and 4.1 mmol/L Glucose Result: What It Means, Next Steps, and When to Seek Care
description: Got a 6.2 mmol/L ketones and 4.1 mmol/L glucose result? Learn what this reading means, euglycemic DKA risks, at-home steps, and when to get emergency care for diabetes.

mainEntity.name: Is 6.2 mmol/L ketones and 4.1 mmol/L glucose a sign of euglycemic DKA?

acceptedAnswer.text: This reading meets the initial lab criteria for suspected euglycemic DKA, which is defined by ketones over 3.0 mmol/L and glucose under 13.9 mmol/L. You should check for DKA symptoms immediately and follow your care team’s protocol, as formal diagnosis requires testing for metabolic acidosis.

mainEntity.name: What immediate steps should I take if I get this ketone and glucose reading?

acceptedAnswer.text: First, confirm the reading with a second test if possible. Type 1 patients should take a small correction dose of rapid-acting insulin and drink sugar-free electrolytes, while Type 2 patients on SGLT2 inhibitors should stop their medication immediately and hydrate. Retest both levels in 30 minutes.

mainEntity.name: Can people with Type 2 diabetes get high ketones with low glucose levels?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, people with Type 2 diabetes taking SGLT2 inhibitors are at high risk for this mismatched reading, even if their glucose stays within normal or low ranges. SGLT2 inhibitors lower blood glucose but do not prevent ketone production during times of stress, illness, or dehydration.

mainEntity.name: When should I seek emergency care for high ketone readings?

acceptedAnswer.text: Seek emergency care immediately if you have ketones over 3.0 mmol/L paired with DKA symptoms like abdominal pain, nausea, rapid shallow breathing, fruity breath, or confusion, regardless of your glucose level. You should also seek care if your ketone levels do not drop within 1 hour of at-home treatment.

mainEntity.name: How often should I test ketones if I’m at risk for this mismatched reading?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you have Type 1 diabetes or take SGLT2 inhibitors, test ketones any time you feel unwell, have a fever, are fasting, or have missed insulin doses. For regular monitoring, test 1-2 times weekly if you are otherwise healthy, per your care team’s guidance.
